name: Line
description: Draws straight edges point to point, healing them into faces the moment a loop closes. The bedrock of SketchUp drafting — used constantly for sketching plans on the ground plane and tracing over imported CAD before pulling walls up.

name: Freehand
description: Draws loose, hand-sketched curves as a chain of small edges. Handy for organic site boundaries, planting outlines or a deliberately sketchy annotation over a formal model.

name: Rectangle
description: Creates a rectangular face from two opposite corners, with exact sizes typed into the Measurements box. The usual starting point for concept massing — draw a footprint, then Push/Pull it into a volume.

name: Rotated Rectangle
description: Draws a rectangle at any angle and on any plane by defining an edge first, rather than aligning to the axes. Useful for buildings set off the grid or faces on sloping ground.

name: Circle
description: Creates a circular face from a centre and radius; the segment count can be typed before or after placing it. Reach for it for columns, roof lights and turning circles — remember SketchUp circles are really polygons, so add segments for smooth curves.

name: Polygon
description: Draws a regular inscribed or circumscribed polygon with a typed number of sides. Unlike Circle, extruding it keeps its edges unsoftened, so it reads as a true faceted prism — good for pavilions, bollards and gazebo plans.

name: Arc
description: Draws an arc from centre, start point and angle, like a compass. Suits setting-out geometry where the centre is known, such as a bay window struck from a fixed point.

name: 2 Point Arc
description: Draws an arc from two endpoints and a bulge distance, and shows tangent inferences in magenta for smooth corner fillets. The everyday arc tool — most designers use it to round plan corners and draw doors' swing geometry.

name: 3 Point Arc
description: Defines an arc through three picked points on its curve. Useful when tracing scanned drawings or survey information where you know points the arc must pass through but not its centre.

name: Pie
description: Draws a closed pie-shaped wedge — an arc plus its two radii — as a single face. Convenient for door swings on plans and for slicing sector diagrams out of circular geometry.

name: Push/Pull
description: Extrudes a face along its normal to add or carve away volume, with exact distances typed in. SketchUp's signature move: pull footprints into massing blocks, push openings through walls, and double-click to repeat the last distance.

name: Push/Pull Copy (Ctrl)
description: Tapping Ctrl (Option on Mac) during Push/Pull leaves the original face behind and extrudes a new slab from it. Ideal for stacking floor plates from one footprint or stepping a terraced form without redrawing.

name: Move
description: Moves entities from a picked base point to a destination, locking to axes with the arrow keys and taking typed distances. Also stretches raw geometry when you grab an edge or vertex, so it doubles as SketchUp's stretch tool.

name: Move Copy (Ctrl)
description: Tapping Ctrl (Option on Mac) while moving duplicates the selection instead of displacing it. This is the standard way to copy anything in the model — furniture, trees, whole buildings — with a precise offset typed afterwards.

name: Linear Array (Move ×/÷)
description: After a Move-copy, typing a value such as 5x repeats the copy five times at the same spacing, while /5 divides the distance into five equal steps. The quickest way to array columns down a grid, balusters along a stair or trees along an avenue.
shortcut: M, then Ctrl, then n× or /n

name: Rotate
description: Rotates a selection about a picked point, with the protractor cursor snapping to the plane it hovers over and exact angles typed in. Also folds raw geometry along an edge, useful for tilting roof planes.

name: Radial Array (Rotate ×/÷)
description: A Rotate-copy followed by typing n× or /n produces a polar array around the rotation centre. Reach for it when placing chairs around a table, treads on a spiral stair or mullions around a drum.
shortcut: Q, then Ctrl, then n× or /n

name: Scale
description: Resizes a selection by dragging its grips, uniformly from the corners or in one direction from face grips, with factors or exact dimensions typed in. Ctrl scales about the centre and negative values mirror — a common trick for flipping components.

name: Offset
description: Copies a face's boundary or a chain of edges parallel to itself at a typed distance, inward or outward. The staple for wall thicknesses in plan, window reveals and path edges — offset the footprint, then Push/Pull the ring.

name: Follow Me
description: Sweeps a profile face along a path of edges to create extrusions that turn corners — think gutters, skirtings, cornices and handrails. Pre-selecting the path then clicking the profile gives the most predictable result; sweeping around a circle also produces lathe-like forms such as domes and balusters.

name: Intersect Faces
description: Draws real edges wherever the selected geometry crosses other faces (With Model, With Selection or With Context). The manual Boolean workhorse in every SketchUp edition — intersect a pitched roof with walls, then erase the waste by hand.

name: Outer Shell
description: Merges overlapping solid groups or components into one solid, discarding all internal faces. Handy for cleaning up massing studies built from overlapping blocks before export or 3D printing.

name: Union
description: A Solid Tools operation that fuses two or more solids into a single solid, keeping any internal voids. Use it to weld a porch into a house block once the composition is settled; requires watertight groups or components.

name: Subtract
description: A Solid Tools operation that removes the first solid from the second and deletes the cutter. The clean way to carve a stair void from a floor slab or bore service openings through a solid wall group.

name: Trim (Solid Tools)
description: Like Subtract, but keeps the cutting solid afterwards. Perfect for notching joists over a beam or letting one repeated component cut many others while remaining in the model.

name: Intersect (Solid Tools)
description: Keeps only the volume shared by the selected solids and discards the rest. Useful for finding the overlap between a massing envelope and a rights-of-light or planning envelope during feasibility work.

name: Split (Solid Tools)
description: Divides overlapping solids along their shared boundaries, keeping every resulting piece as its own solid. Good for phasing studies or splitting a building volume at a party wall while retaining both halves.

name: Eraser
description: Deletes edges (and the faces they support) by clicking or scrubbing across them. With Ctrl it softens edges instead, and with Shift it hides them — three cleanup behaviours in one tool.

name: Soften Edges
description: Softens and smooths edges across a selection by angle threshold, so faceted surfaces shade as continuous curves and coplanar joins disappear. Essential after Follow Me or imported meshes to make curved forms render cleanly.

name: Weld Edges
description: Joins a selected chain of edges or arcs into a single continuous curve entity. Do this before Follow Me or Push/Pull along a path so the result behaves as one sweep rather than many segments.

name: Flip
description: Mirrors a selection across a chosen plane using on-screen handles, with a copy toggle for making handed pairs. The modern replacement for the old Flip Along commands — ideal for mirroring a staircase or producing left- and right-hand door components.

name: Explode
description: Breaks a group, component or curve back into its raw constituent geometry one level at a time. Use it deliberately — exploding imported CAD or Warehouse components floods the model with loose edges that are hard to manage.

name: Select
description: Picks entities singly, by left-to-right window or right-to-left crossing box, with Shift and Ctrl to add or subtract. Double-click selects a face with its edges; triple-click grabs all connected geometry — the fastest way to grab a whole loose object.

name: Select All
description: Selects everything visible in the current editing context, respecting hidden geometry and locked objects. Typical before a whole-model move to the origin or a global tag change.

name: Select None
description: Clears the current selection without clicking into empty space, which matters in a crowded model where a stray click could pick something. A small habit that prevents accidental edits.

name: Invert Selection
description: Swaps selected and unselected entities within the current context. Often quicker to pick the few things you want to keep, invert, then delete or hide everything else.

name: Make Component
description: Wraps the selection into a named, reusable component definition; editing one instance updates every copy. The right choice for anything repeated — windows, doors, furniture, structural bays — and the backbone of an efficient SketchUp file.

name: Make Group
description: Isolates the selection inside a group so its geometry stops sticking to everything around it. Use groups for one-off elements like a site plinth or a unique wall run; use components when the object repeats.

name: Edit Group/Component
description: Opens a group or component for editing (double-click does the same), fading the rest of the model while you work inside its context. Edits to a component instance propagate to all copies unless it is first made unique.

name: Close Group/Component
description: Steps back out of the group or component you are editing, one nesting level at a time; clicking in empty space or pressing Esc does the same. Knowing which context you are in prevents geometry ending up in the wrong container.

name: Lock
description: Locks the selected groups or components so they show a red highlight and cannot be moved or edited. Lock the surveyed site, imported CAD reference or party-wall geometry so design changes can't disturb them.

name: Unlock All
description: Releases every locked object in the model in one action (Edit > Unlock, alongside unlocking just the selection). Useful at the end of a design stage when reference geometry finally needs adjusting.

name: Hide
description: Hides the selected entities from view without deleting them, decluttering the scene while you work behind or inside something. Hidden objects can be revealed via View > Hidden Objects or brought back with Unhide.

name: Unhide All
description: Restores everything hidden in the current context (Edit > Unhide offers Selected, Last and All). Run it before issuing a model so nothing is accidentally missing from exports.

name: Hide Rest of Model
description: While editing a group or component, hides everything outside the editing context instead of merely fading it (View > Component Edit). An informal isolate mode that makes detailed work inside a cluttered model far easier.

name: Outliner
description: A tree view of every group and component in the model, showing nesting, names and lock or hidden states. Use it to navigate deep hierarchies, rename containers and restructure a model the way you'd manage layers in a drawing.

name: Tags
description: SketchUp's visibility layers (renamed from Layers in 2020): assign whole groups and components to tags, then switch categories like furniture, structure or existing/proposed on and off per scene. Best practice keeps raw geometry untagged and tags only containers.

name: Entity Info
description: Shows and edits the selection's properties — tag, name, dimensions, segment count, face area, volume of solids — plus toggles for hidden, locked and shadow casting. The quickest place to check whether a group is a true solid or to read a floor plate's area.

name: Tape Measure
description: Measures distances and, when dragged from an edge or point, creates dashed guide lines and guide points for setting out. Typing a new value after measuring between two points can rescale the whole model — the classic fix for imported drawings at the wrong size.

name: Protractor
description: Measures angles and places angled guide lines from a vertex and reference direction. Typical for setting out roof pitches, splayed walls and ramps before drawing real geometry against the guides.

name: Dimensions
description: Places linear, radial and diameter dimensions that stay associated with the model and update as geometry changes. Fine for quick studies and workshop drawings, though most formal dimensioning is done in LayOut.

name: Axes
description: Relocates and reorients the model's red, green and blue drawing axes. Align them to an angled wing of a building so rectangles, inferences and Move directions follow that grid instead of the world axes.

name: Text
description: Places screen-facing labels, either leadered to an entity (auto-filling its name, area or length) or floating as screen notes. Useful for annotating design options and room names during early studies.

name: 3D Text
description: Generates extruded or flat text as real geometry in a component. Reach for it for signage, carved lettering, entrance branding on visuals or scale-figure labels on massing models.

name: Section Plane
description: Places a live cutting plane through the model to reveal interiors; planes can be named, reversed, moved with standard tools and saved per scene. The foundation of plan and section workflows — pair one with a scene, then reference it in LayOut.

name: Section Cuts
description: Toggles whether active section planes actually slice the display, independently of whether the plane widgets themselves are shown (View > Section Cuts and View > Section Planes). Scenes remember both states, so one model can hold plans, sections and full views together.

name: Section Fill
description: Fills the cut faces of a section with a solid poché colour (set in the style) instead of leaving hollow outlines. Makes plans and sections read properly, showing walls and slabs as solid cut material.

name: Delete Guides
description: Removes every guide line and guide point in the current context in one go. Run it after setting-out is done so construction guides don't clutter exports and LayOut viewports.

name: Orbit
description: Rotates the camera around the model in 3D; the middle mouse button invokes it temporarily from any tool. Holding Ctrl frees the camera from the gravity-locked horizon for unusual angles.

name: Pan
description: Slides the camera parallel to the screen without changing the viewing angle; Shift with the middle mouse button does the same mid-tool. Used constantly alongside Orbit when working across a large site model.

name: Zoom
description: Moves the camera towards or away from the model by dragging, though most users simply roll the scroll wheel, which zooms about the cursor. With the tool active, typing a value like 45deg sets the field of view.

name: Zoom Extents
description: Frames the entire model in the view. Also a diagnostic: if Zoom Extents flings the camera miles away, some stray geometry is lurking far from the origin and should be hunted down.

name: Zoom Window
description: Zooms to fill the screen with a rectangle you drag around an area of interest. Quicker than scroll-zooming when jumping straight to one corner of a large site model.

name: Previous
description: Steps the camera back to the previous view, like an undo for navigation only. Handy after an accidental orbit or zoom has lost a carefully composed angle that wasn't saved as a scene.

name: Standard Views
description: Snaps the camera to Top, Bottom, Front, Back, Left, Right or Iso. Combine Top with Parallel Projection for a true plan view, or Front with it for a straight elevation ready to export.

name: Perspective
description: The default camera mode, with converging lines and a realistic sense of depth. Use it for design views, walkthroughs and visuals — anything meant to be experienced rather than measured.

name: Parallel Projection
description: Switches to an orthographic camera with no perspective convergence, so parallel edges stay parallel. Essential for plans, elevations and axonometric exports where drawings must scale correctly.

name: Two-Point Perspective
description: Forces vertical edges to stay truly vertical, as in classic architectural photography and hand-drawn perspectives. Switch to it just before composing presentation views so towers don't appear to lean.

name: Position Camera
description: Places the camera at a clicked point at standing eye height (or a typed height), facing a chosen direction. The starting move for verified street views and interior eye-level shots, usually followed by Look Around.

name: Walk
description: Moves the camera through the model at a fixed eye height with collision detection, climbing stairs and stopping at walls. Use it to test spatial sequences — approach, threshold, room-to-room flow — from a person's point of view.

name: Look Around
description: Pivots the camera in place, like turning your head from a fixed standing position. Pairs with Position Camera to scan a room or streetscape from a single verified viewpoint.

name: Field of View
description: Sets the camera's viewing angle by dragging or typing a value in degrees or as a lens focal length in millimetres. Widen it for tight interiors, narrow it towards 35–50 mm equivalents for natural-looking exterior views.

name: Match New Photo
description: Calibrates a camera to a photograph by aligning vanishing-point bars, so you can model over the image or composite a proposal into its real context. Valued for extensions and infill work where the model must sit convincingly in a site photo.

name: Scenes
description: Saves named snapshots of camera position, style, tag visibility, section states and shadows, shown as clickable tabs above the viewport. Scenes drive everything downstream: LayOut viewports, animations and consistent presentation views.

name: Add Scene
description: Captures the current view and display settings as a new scene tab (View > Animation > Add Scene). Remember to right-click and Update a scene after changing it, or the tab will snap back to its saved state.

name: Paint Bucket
description: Applies the active material to faces, or to whole groups and components in one click. Shift repaints every face sharing the old material, and Ctrl repaints connected faces only — big time-savers when swapping a facade treatment.

name: Sample Material (Alt)
description: Holding Alt (Cmd on Mac) with Paint Bucket turns the cursor into an eyedropper that picks up the material under it, ready to apply elsewhere. The fastest way to reuse an existing finish without hunting through the Materials tray.

name: Materials
description: The library and editor for colours and textures: browse collections, import images as materials, and adjust tint, size and opacity. Its In Model tab lists every material used in the file — the place to purge duplicates and manage a palette.

name: Styles
description: Controls how the model is drawn — edge weight and extensions, face rendering, background and sky, watermarks and section fill colour. Designers keep a crisp working style and a sketchy or presentation style, switching per scene.

name: Face Style
description: Switches face rendering between Wireframe, Hidden Line, Shaded, Shaded with Textures and Monochrome (View > Face Style). Monochrome is the honest mode for design reviews and for spotting reversed blue back faces before export.

name: X-ray
description: Makes all faces semi-transparent so you can see and snap through walls and floors (View > Face Style > X-ray). Useful for checking alignment between storeys or picking geometry buried inside a building.

name: Back Edges
description: Displays hidden edges behind faces as dashed lines without making faces transparent. A lighter-touch alternative to X-ray when you need to reference concealed structure while modelling.

name: Hidden Geometry
description: Reveals softened and hidden edges as dashed hatching so curved surfaces show their real facet structure. Turn it on to select and edit individual facets of a dome, terrain or swept form.

name: Shadows
description: Toggles real sun shadows in the viewport, driven by the model's geolocation, date and time. Instant daylight sanity-checks: overshadowing of neighbours, depth of a brise-soleil, sun in a courtyard at the equinox.

name: Shadow Settings
description: The panel with date and time sliders, light and dark intensity, and whether shadows fall on faces, on the ground or from edges. Scrub the time slider through a design-day to run a quick solar study, saving key moments as scenes.

name: Fog
description: Fades distant geometry towards a background colour with adjustable near and far distances. A cheap atmospheric-depth effect that helps foreground proposals stand out from context in massing views.

name: Components
description: Browses component definitions — those in the model, local collections and 3D Warehouse results — for dragging into the scene. The In Model tab is also where definitions are reloaded from or saved back to external files for a shared office library.

name: 3D Warehouse
description: Trimble's free online library of user- and manufacturer-made models, searchable from inside SketchUp (File > 3D Warehouse > Get Models). Great for entourage, furniture and sanitaryware — but check polygon counts and purge heavy downloads to keep files lean.

name: Interact
description: Clicks Dynamic Components to trigger their scripted behaviours — opening a door, cycling a configuration, animating a drawer. Only affects components authored with dynamic attributes; ordinary geometry ignores it.

name: Component Options
description: Shows the user-facing controls of a selected Dynamic Component — dropdowns and fields for size, configuration or finish defined by its author. How a designer resizes a parametric window or cabinet without touching raw geometry.

name: Component Attributes
description: The authoring panel for Dynamic Components, where attributes, formulas and behaviours are defined (Pro feature). Used to build parametric families — stairs that recalculate treads, fencing that repeats posts to suit length.

name: Sandbox: From Contours
description: Skins a triangulated TIN surface over stacked contour lines (Draw > Sandbox). The standard route from imported survey or OS contour data to a 3D site terrain ready for massing studies.

name: Sandbox: From Scratch
description: Creates a flat rectangular terrain grid of a set cell size, ready to be sculpted. Use it when no survey exists and you need a quick, editable ground plane for landform sketching.

name: Sandbox: Smoove
description: Sculpts terrain by pushing and pulling vertices within a soft circular radius, like moulding clay (Tools > Sandbox). Shape berms, valleys and building platforms on a Sandbox grid or TIN.

name: New
description: Starts a fresh model from the default or a chosen template. Templates set units and style, so an office metric-millimetre template keeps every project starting consistently.

name: Open
description: Opens an existing .skp model. SketchUp files are versioned — 2025 can open older files, but colleagues on older releases may need a back-saved copy via Save As.

name: Save
description: Saves the model; SketchUp also keeps an automatic backup (.skb on Windows, filename~.skp on Mac) alongside recovery auto-saves. Save little and often — heavy Boolean and terrain work is where crashes strike.

name: Save As
description: Saves under a new name or location, and can write older .skp versions for collaborators on previous releases. The tool for milestone copies at each design stage.

name: Save A Copy As
description: Writes a snapshot copy to disk while you carry on working in the current file, which stays the active document. Handy for issuing a record copy mid-session without switching files.

name: Import
description: Brings external files into the model: DWG/DXF site and floor plans, images to trace or use as textures, and 3D formats such as IFC, DAE and STL (format support varies by edition). Imported CAD arrives as a component — keep it grouped and locked as reference.

name: Export 2D Graphic
description: Exports the current view as a raster image (PNG, JPG, TIFF) or 2D vector (PDF, EPS, DWG/DXF) at a chosen resolution. Set up a parallel-projection scene first to export elevations that redraw cleanly, or a styled perspective for report images.

name: Export 3D Model
description: Writes the model out to 3D formats including DWG/DXF, DAE (Collada), FBX, OBJ, IFC, STL and glTF, depending on edition. The hand-off point to consultants, render engines, game engines and 3D printers.

name: Send to LayOut
description: Pushes the saved model into LayOut, SketchUp's companion drawing-sheet application, creating a linked viewport on a chosen template. The bridge from model to titled, scaled, dimensioned drawing sets that update when the model does.

name: Print
description: Prints the current view, with a to-scale option available in parallel projection. Serviceable for quick check prints; proper scaled sheets are better produced through LayOut.

name: Add Location
description: Geolocates the model on real map data and can import a snapshot of terrain and imagery for the site (File > Geo-location). Accurate location makes shadow studies meaningful and places the model correctly for context tools.

name: Generate Report
description: Extracts component and attribute data from the model into a configurable tabular report (CSV) — counts, sizes, prices from dynamic attributes. Useful for door schedules, planting counts and rough quantity take-offs.

name: Purge Unused
description: Deletes unused component definitions, materials, styles and tags from the file (Model Info > Statistics > Purge Unused). Run it after deleting Warehouse downloads — it routinely shrinks bloated files dramatically.

name: Model Info
description: The model's settings hub: units and precision, dimension and text styling, geolocation, animation transitions, statistics and file fixing. Set units here first — it governs every typed measurement in the file.

name: Preferences
description: Application-wide options: keyboard shortcut editing, autosave interval, file locations, graphics settings and workspace choices. The Shortcuts page is where power users bind their most-used tools to single keys.

name: LayOut: SketchUp Model Viewport
description: In LayOut, an inserted SketchUp model appears as a viewport tied to a saved scene, with per-viewport scale, style and rendering mode (raster, vector, hybrid). Because it stays linked, updating the model refreshes every sheet in the set.

name: LayOut: Scaled Drawing
description: A LayOut drawing area where 2D linework is drawn at a true architectural scale, such as 1:50 or 1:100. Used for details, setting-out diagrams and embellishing model viewports with drafted information that measures correctly on the sheet.

name: LayOut: Dimensions
description: LayOut's linear and angular dimension tools snap to model geometry inside viewports and read true model measurements at the viewport's scale. The proper home for drawing-set dimensioning, updating when the linked model changes.

name: Undo
description: Steps back through recent modelling operations. Note it does not undo camera moves — use Previous for that — which keeps design experimentation fast and low-risk.

name: Redo
description: Reinstates the last undone operation. Useful when flicking back and forth between two states of a design move to judge which reads better.

name: Cut
description: Removes the selection to the clipboard for pasting elsewhere, including into another open SketchUp window. Combined with Paste In Place, it is the standard way to move geometry into a different group or component context.

name: Copy
description: Copies the selection to the clipboard, ready to paste into this or another model. For copies within the same view, Move-copy with Ctrl is usually faster and more precise.

name: Paste
description: Places clipboard contents attached to the cursor for positioning with a click. Works between SketchUp windows, making it easy to lift parts of one project into another.

name: Paste In Place
description: Pastes clipboard geometry at exactly its original coordinates rather than on the cursor. The essential partner to Cut when restructuring — move geometry between groups, components or files without it shifting a millimetre.

name: Delete
description: Removes the selected entities from the model. Deleting an edge deletes the faces it bounds, so check what disappears — Undo is always one keystroke away.

name: Extension Warehouse
description: Trimble's curated store for installing SketchUp extensions from inside the application. The first stop when native tools run out — renderers, drawing aids, terrain tools and fabrication helpers.

name: Extension Manager
description: Enables, disables, updates and side-loads installed extensions (.rbz files). Disable heavyweight plugins you aren't using — a lean load-out keeps SketchUp starting and running faster.

name: Instructor
description: A context-sensitive help panel that animates how the currently active tool works, including its modifier keys. Worth keeping open while learning — it surfaces the Ctrl and Shift behaviours beginners miss.

name: Large Tool Set
description: A two-column toolbar (View > Toolbars) exposing the full core tool collection — drawing, modification, camera, section and walkthrough tools — without menu-diving. Most learners dock it while they build shortcut muscle memory.

name: JointPushPull
description: Extends Push/Pull to curved and multiple faces at once, with normal, vector and thickening modes. The go-to extension for giving curtain-wall glazing, vaults and curved shells a real material thickness.

name: RoundCorner
description: Fillets and chamfers edges and corners of 3D geometry with round, sharp or bevel profiles. Softens the toy-like sharpness of raw SketchUp models — eased worktops, bullnosed steps, bevelled panels.

name: Curic Section
description: A professional sectioning extension that generates filled, hatched and lineweight-controlled section cuts well beyond native section fill. Popular for producing presentation-quality plans and sections directly from the model.

name: Import/Export STL
description: The open-source SketchUp STL extension adds STL import and export under the File menu for 3D-printing workflows. Check geometry is a watertight solid in Entity Info before exporting, or the print will fail. Recent SketchUp versions also ship native STL support, so the extension mainly serves older installs.
